title: Behavior from behavior
summary: A method can take lambdas in and hand a new lambda back.

say.never: Making a lambda is like writing a recipe card: nothing gets cooked yet. The code inside only runs when someone calls its method. Here, nothing prints on the first line. It prints on the last one.
say.bit: Creating a lambda runs nothing. Its code runs each time its method is called.

say.never: Since a lambda is a value, a method can take one as a parameter and hand a new one back. `twice` takes any greeter and returns a greeter that runs it two times. The new lambda calls the old one *inside* its body, so it still doesn't run anything until someone calls `greet`.
say.bit: A method can take a lambda and return a new lambda that calls it.

steps.title: In your lesson: Lambdas in, lambda out

say.never: `chain(first, second)` returns a new filter. Given a speed, it runs `first` on it, then runs `second` on that answer. Write it inside out: `first.apply(speed)` goes inside `second.apply( )`. Don't call `apply` outside the lambda: there's no speed yet when `chain` runs.
say.bit: `chain` returns a lambda that calls `second.apply(...)` on `first.apply(speed)`.

say.never: Your turn! Make `chain` return a lambda that runs `first`, then `second` on the result. `chain(half(), invert())` should turn `0.8` into `-0.4`.
